idiom_name: contravariant validator value (input -> verdict) with contramap/divide/conquer/choose/lose combinators
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: represent a check as a value from input to verdict (Validator[A] = A => Verdict), never as a method on the checked type. Four combinators cover the structure: contramap adapts an existing validator to a new input type through a pure projection (b => a); conquer is the validator that accepts everything; divide splits one input into independent parts, runs a validator on each and combines the verdicts with the verdict monoid so all failures survive; choose routes the input to one of two validators via a case split (a => Either b c), with lose for the uninhabited branch. Keep the verdict type explicit - reason plus path plus rule id - because the combinators say how verdicts combine, not what a verdict is. Accumulation is best modeled with an applicative functor (Validated, Validation) rather than a monadic one (Either, Result).
code_sketch:
Validator[A] = A => Verdict                 # the carrier
contramap : (B => A) => Validator[A] => Validator[B]
conquer   : Validator[A]                   # accepts everything
divide    : (A => (B, C)) => Validator[B] => Validator[C] => Validator[A]
choose    : (A => Either[B, C]) => Validator[B] => Validator[C] => Validator[A]
# verdict monoid: combine reasons, never short-circuit
pitfalls: Returning a bare boolean (or Unit) from a validator destroys the reason and the field path: the composed rule can then only say 'invalid'.
Combining with a monadic bind (Either/Result flatMap) instead of the applicative divide silently switches to fail-fast semantics and drops the remaining failures.
Validators that touch I/O, the clock or global state stop being reusable rules and cannot be tested in isolation.

In languages with async support, mixing sync and async validators (e.g., flatMap on an async check) silently drops concurrent validations and reverts to sequential fail-fast even when using an accumulating type.

Schema definition libraries (Zod, pydantic, FluentValidation) often use mutable builder patterns internally; mutating a shared schema definition from multiple threads produces non-deterministic verdicts.

In TypeScript, Zod's `.refine()` and `.superRefine()` produce continuable errors (all checks run) by default, but `.transform()` runs after validation and may receive partial data - relying on transformed values in a `.refine()` without understanding the execution order silently ignores errors.

Wrong move: registering DI-resolved validators that inject scoped services (DbContext, repositories) as singletons -> the captured scoped dependency leaks across requests and produces cross-request state or deadlocks under load -> instead default validators to a scoped lifetime, or keep them pure and inject the already-computed fact through contramap.

Wrong move: relying on a framework's cascade/short-circuit knob (FluentValidation CascadeMode, schema-library abortEarly flags) on a rule set that was designed to accumulate -> the same composed rules silently report one error per submission and the semantics change whenever someone edits the mode, not the code -> instead fix the accumulation strategy in the combinator itself (divide always runs both sides) and reserve fail-fast for deliberately short-circuiting pipelines.

Wrong move: expressing every cross-field and single-field rule as inline .refine()/.superRefine() lambdas on each endpoint schema -> hundreds of lines of copy-pasted predicates that drift per site and share no rule id -> instead extract each rule once as a named reusable validator, compose with divide/and or schema merging, and keep refine only for rules that genuinely need the whole object.
